newsitem.title: GREECE: New wave of anti-austerity strikes hits Greece.
newsitem.headline: New wave of anti-austerity strikes hits Greece.

text.p: Greek teachers and workers go on strike this week against the socialist government's tough incomes and tax policies, joining seamen and civil aviation staff whose walkouts have disrupted Greek transport.
A seven-day strike by seamen, affecting all ships with Greek crews, has been marked by clashes with special coast guard forces and has kept most vessels idle at ports.
Striking civil aviation staff protesting against wage and bonus cuts have disrupted flights at airports around Greece.

Air traffic controllers cancelled a four-hour work stoppage on Sunday to hold negotiations after a similar walkout on Friday caused chaos at airports. Civil aviation electrical engineers continued a three-day strike that ends on Monday.
High school teachers begin an indefinite strike on Monday to press for better pay, while Greece biggest labour confederation (GSEE) has announced a 24-hour walkout for Thursday.

It is the second wave of strikes to hit Greece since the socialist government, which won elections in September, launched a tough economic policy to bring the nation closer to its European Union partners.
Technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis said his budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, was necessary bitter medicine for the country and has turned down all union demands.

He successfully stared down a crippling farmers' blockade that virtually cut the country in two in December but farmers are threatening to block highways with their tractors again if demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts are not met by February 4.

"The government will not tolerate blackmail and arbitrary actions which violate the freedom of citizens and strike at the country's fragile economy," Simitis told parliament on Friday during a discussion on agriculture.
Farmers have also been hit by the seamen's strike, with hundreds of trucks lined up waiting for ferries to sail and tonnes of produce rotting since last week.
On the island of Crete, farmers tried to set fire to mooring lines, demanding that some ships be allowed to transport perishables to the mainland.
The government announced two air carriers and two navy ships would be sent to the island to bring back goods destined for export.

The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO), which wants better pensions, benefits and measures against unemployment, on Friday defied a court decision declaring its walkout illegal and said it would end the strike on Tuesday as scheduled.
A Piraeus court ordered the seamen to return to work or face fines and arrest. Police said there had been no detentions so far.
"Our strike will go on because it is the only way to safeguard our rights and satisfy our just demands," PNO general secretary Yannis Halas said.
